title: Sharpen a new pencil in a crank sharpener and lay it back in its rest
instruction: Sharpen the yellow pencil in the crank sharpener: push it into the hole and turn the crank forward (its knob going over the top, away from the robot) until the pencil goes in no further. Then pull the pencil out, lay it back in both notches of its wooden rest and let go.
context: Most people have sharpened a pencil in a crank sharpener at school, at home or in an office; over 2 billion pencils are used in the US a year. The cutters orbit the pencil and only take wood from an end pressed onto them, so one hand must keep the pencil pressed in while the cut draws it 24 mm deeper, about 1.5 mm a turn over 16 turns, and the other carries the crank knob round a 90 mm vertical circle against the cutting drag. Pushed without cranking, the pencil stops dead; held still while cranked, it soon runs free of the cutters. Hardest ability: keeping the pencil's end on the cutters as they take wood, coaxial in a bore with 1 mm a side, while the other gripper turns the knob against 4.4 N, then pulling it straight out and laying it in two V notches. Nearest board task: a bench can opener whose lever is held still while the other hand cranks; here the held part moves 24 mm along its axis with the cut (the lever, 0 mm).
setup: Positions in mm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table). Sharpener: X-ACTO KS 1031 manual sharpener, steel and black plastic, 121 x 70 x 108 mm, 295 g, screwed with two wood screws onto a pine 2x4 offcut (38 x 89 x 150 mm, centre x 300, y -20) clamped to the table, so its crank clears the table. Bore axis (the line the pencil follows into the cutters): horizontal along y at x 300, z 118. Guide dial face at y +40.5, facing the robot's left, set to its 7/16 in (11.1 mm) hole, built as a 12.3 mm octagonal bore in two rings: the dial ring (y +34.5 to +37.5, behind a 45 degree lead-in 3 mm deep) and the cutter carriage entry (y +12.5 to +16.5, behind a 1.5 mm lead-in). The cutting front, where the pencil's square end first meets the cutters, starts at y +10.5. Crank, coaxial with the pencil on the far face (y -80.5): a steel hub 16 mm across, a steel arm 45 mm from axis to knob pin, and a black plastic knob 20 mm across and 50 mm long that spins freely on its pin; crank bearing friction 0.05 N m; while the pencil is pressed on the cutting front and the point is not yet complete, turning the crank forward takes 0.15 N m more (the cutting drag, rising with crank speed to its full value at 0.5 rad/s and above), 0.2 N m in all, 4.4 N at the knob. At the start the knob points straight up, its centre at (300, -121.5, 163). Forward is clockwise seen from the crank side: the knob goes over the top away from the robot. Pencil: Dixon Ticonderoga My First, no eraser (33036), round, 10.3 mm (13/32 in) across, 166 mm (6.52 in) long, incense cedar with a graphite core, yellow, about 9 g, new and unsharpened: both ends cut square. It lies along y on a desk pen rest, centre (220, 220, 30.3). Pen rest: pine, 25 g, taped to the table: a base strip 30 x 130 x 8 mm centred at (220, 220) with two V blocks (30 x 16 x 22 mm, a 90 degree notch 7 mm deep) at y 175 and 265; the pencil's axis sits 30.3 mm above the table. How the cut is built in the simulator: the cutting front is a 14 mm disc on a sprung feeler (5 mm travel, 1,000 N/m, so a 2 N press pushes it in 2 mm), carried by a slide held at the cut depth by a stiff drive (50,000 N/m), so the pencil gets at most 5 mm, plus 1 mm per 50 N, past the uncut wood. In each control step in which the pencil's end, through both rings and within 1.5 mm of the axis, is within 1 mm of the disc, pushing the feeler in at least 2 mm, and the crank turns forward past the furthest angle it has reached within the last turn, the slide's target moves 1.5 mm deeper per crank turn, to 24 mm (16 turns), where the point is complete and the pencil stop ends the cut. Real counterpart: the KS itself, whose cutters cut only a pressed pencil end, so the pencil advances only as wood is removed, and whose crank turns harder while they cut; the drag is the work to shave the 1.3 cm3 of wood and graphite a 24 mm point removes, over 16 turns. The layout is the same in every trial.
scoring: Cut depth D is how far the cutting front's slide has moved in, 0 to 24 mm. It grows only as the setup states (the pencil's end, through both rings, held pressed on the cutting front while the crank turns forward past its furthest angle within the last turn, 1.5 mm per turn) and never shrinks; turning backward, cranking with the pencil loose, resting or held off the front, and pushing without cranking add nothing. Credit is the highest tier reached; each is a stage of the cut. 0.25: D reached 6 mm (four pressed forward turns). 0.5: D reached 12 mm. 0.75: D reached 24 mm (the point is complete). 1.0: D is 24 mm and, at the end, the whole pencil is at least 10 mm clear of the sharpener; it lies in both notches of its rest (its axis within 3 mm sideways and 2 mm in height of the notch seat at both V blocks); it has been released on every step of the last 1 s (every finger point of both grippers at least 30 mm from the pencil; grippers whose fingers cannot be read count as holding it); and it has moved 2 mm or less over that 1 s. Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial, read on the pencil with a ruler and from the video: 0.25, a cut cone at least 6 mm long at the pencil's end (the flat left at its tip at most 7.8 mm across); 0.5, a cone at least 12 mm long, the flat no wider than half the pencil (5.2 mm); 0.75, a cone 24 mm long and the graphite brought to a point (no flat left); 1.0, a side photo of the pencil down in both V notches and video frames showing both grippers 3 cm clear and nothing moving for the last second. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the 1.0 state has held for 1 s.
fidelity: PhysX rigid bodies, 20 Hz control. Simplified: helical cutters are a disc on a 5 mm, 1,000 N/m feeler and a 50,000 N/m slide that moves 1.5 mm deeper per forward turn while the end pushes the feeler in at least 2 mm; the cut shows as the pencil advancing 24 mm, its end stays square. Crank: hinge, 0.05 N m friction, 0.15 N m drag while pressed. 11.1 mm hole: a 12.3 mm octagonal bore. Crank radius, knob size, bore layout, cone length, turns to a point and both torques are our estimates.
reset_notes: Each real trial uses up a pencil: start every trial with a new, unsharpened My First pencil without eraser (166 mm long, both ends square); never re-use a sharpened pencil. Check the dial is at its 7/16 in hole. Empty the shavings drawer every ten trials. Lay the pencil in both notches of the rest, centred between them, and turn the crank knob straight up. In the simulator the cutting slide, feeler, crank and pencil return to their start poses.
